title: The problem isn't a lack of data. It's not knowing how to turn data into decisions.
description: Having a dashboard doesn't make you data-driven. How to start from the decision, tell information apart from insight and use visualization as part of the process.

related.title: Clint Acquire
related.body: In practice: a landing page and a conversational flow that brought in 79% of sales demand.

lines: Today, almost any digital product can generate a huge amount of data.
We have more information than ever.
But having lots of data doesn't necessarily mean making better decisions.
In my view, one of the biggest challenges for product teams today isn't finding new data.
It's knowing what to do with the data we already have.
data.list: Clicks, conversions, sessions, retention, drop-off, time on product, surveys, reviews, tickets, session recordings...

blocks.text: Having a dashboard doesn't make you data-driven
It's common to find companies with dashboards full of charts and numbers.
Everything seems to be tracked.
But when a simple question comes up:
“What should we do with this information?”
There isn't always an answer.

data.lead: A dashboard can show that conversion dropped 15%.
causes: It could be a usability problem
It could be a change in traffic
It could be a price change
It could be a technical issue
data.extra: It could be a change in user behavior.
data.b: We need to investigate to understand why.

blocks.text: Data doesn't replace research
This is a point I consider really important for anyone working in UX and Product Design.
There's a tendency to put quantitative data and qualitative research on opposite sides.
As if we had to choose between:
“What do the numbers say?”
or
“What do the users say?”
In practice, we can use both.
Imagine Analytics shows that 60% of users drop off at a certain step.
That data point matters.
But we still have a question:
Why are they dropping off?
So we can talk to users, run usability tests, analyze sessions and observe behavior.
Maybe we'll find that the problem is a piece of information that isn't clear.
Or a field that makes people feel unsure.
Or a step that seems unnecessary.
Now we have a lot more context to make a decision.
Not every data point needs to become a metric
Another thing that can happen is turning everything into a KPI.
Not every piece of information needs to be a business metric.
Some information is there to raise questions.
Some helps find problems.
Some helps validate hypotheses.
And some really does need to track product performance.
What matters is knowing the role of that data.
Before asking:
“What's our metric?”
It might be better to ask:
“What decision do we need to make?”
From there we can figure out which information we actually need.
Starting from the decision changes everything
Imagine the team wants to improve onboarding.

blocks.caption: One question turns a crowded dashboard into the few metrics that lead to a decision.

blocks.text: Instead of starting by building a dashboard with dozens of metrics, we can start with a question:
“Why aren't new users reaching the first moment of value?”
From that question, we can look at:

items: behavior of users who complete the process;

blocks.text: Now the data has a purpose.
It's helping answer a question.
And that answer can lead to a product decision.
Data visualization is part of the process too
This is where a skill comes in that I think matters more and more for Product Designers.
Knowing how to turn data into a visual story.
A chart shouldn't exist just because it “looks nice on the dashboard”.
The visualization needs to help someone understand something.

data.lead: A good dashboard should let a person quickly answer:
questions: What decision can I make from this?
close: If we have to spend several minutes staring at charts to figure out what's going on, maybe the problem isn't the data.
It might be the way it's being presented.

blocks.text: There's a difference between information and insight
The difference seems small, but it changes the conversation quite a bit.

blocks.caption: More data doesn't mean more clarity.

data.info: The conversion rate dropped from 8% to 5%.
data.insight: Conversion dropped mainly among users on mobile after the new form was launched.
data.l3: The second one already starts pointing toward an investigation.
data.test: Tests show that mobile users are struggling to fill in the second field of the form.
data.l5: Now we have a clearer hypothesis.
data.l6: And from it we can think about a solution.
data.l7: This path is much more useful:
data.chain: Data → Context → Insight → Hypothesis → Decision → Experiment → Result

blocks.text: The Product Designer's role
I believe Product Designers don't need to be data science experts.

items: But we do need to know how to work with data
We need to be able to ask questions

blocks.text: And above all, turn that information into design decisions.
That changes a lot about how we present our work.
Instead of:
“We made a new layout.”
We can say:
“We spotted a conversion drop at this step, investigated user behavior, found a point of friction and created a solution to test that hypothesis.”
The difference isn't just in how we tell the story.
It's in how we think about the work.
More data doesn't mean more clarity
Maybe this is one of the biggest problems right now.
We have tools to measure practically everything.
But measuring everything can have the opposite effect.
A good data process shouldn't generate more questions with no direction.
It should help the team ask better questions.
Because in the end, a product doesn't just need information.
It needs better decisions.
And maybe the real meaning of being data-driven isn't having lots of data.
It's knowing how to use the right data, at the right moment, to make a decision.
